questions.def: "Few" means not many, suitable for countable nouns like "applicants".
questions.question: ___ of the applicants possessed the required qualifications.

questions.def: "Minority" refers to a smaller portion of something uncountable (data).
questions.question: Only a ___ of the research data supports the initial hypothesis.

questions.def: "Much" is for uncountable nouns; use "many" with "students".
questions.question: Much of the students are involved in extracurricular activities.

questions.def: "A number of" precedes plural nouns and takes a plural verb.
questions.question: A ___ of errors were identified in the report.

questions.def: "Little" is used with uncountable nouns like "research".
questions.question: ___ research has been conducted on the long-term effects.

questions.def: "Most" means the majority and is followed by "of" and the noun.
questions.question: ___ of the evidence points to a different conclusion.

questions.def: "Every" requires a singular noun: "every student".
questions.question: Every students must submit their assignments on time.

questions.def: "Number" is used for countable items like "participants".
questions.question: Only a small ___ of participants completed the study.

questions.def: "None" means not any and is used with uncountable nouns.
questions.question: ___ of the information provided was relevant to the investigation.

questions.def: "Several" means more than two but not many, for countable items.
questions.question: ___ of the committee members were in agreement.

questions.def: "Amount" is used with uncountable nouns like "funding".
questions.question: A significant ___ of funding is needed for the research.

questions.def: "Some" implies a portion of the data is available.
questions.question: ___ of the data is publicly available.

questions.def: "Scant" suggests a very small, insufficient amount of evidence.
questions.question: There is ___ evidence to support this claim.

questions.def: "The number" refers to a specific count and takes a singular verb.
questions.question: The ___ of participants is expected to increase.

questions.def: "Several" means more than two, but not many, with countable nouns.
questions.question: ___ students attended the optional lecture.

questions.def: "Fraction" represents a portion of an uncountable noun (budget).
questions.question: Only a ___ of the budget remains unspent.

questions.def: "A little" cannot quantify countable nouns like "students"; use "a few".
questions.question: A little of the students are from overseas.

questions.def: "Amount" is used with uncountable nouns, such as "time".
questions.question: A considerable ___ of time was spent on data analysis.

questions.def: "Neither" implies that two (and only two) interviewees were not suitable.
questions.question: ___ of the interviewees were deemed suitable for the position.

questions.def: "Sizeable" means a fairly large proportion.
questions.question: A ___ proportion of the population supports the new policy.

questions.def: "Number" is used for countable nouns like "complaints".
questions.question: The ___ of complaints has decreased significantly.

questions.def: "Several" means more than two but not many, with countable nouns.
questions.question: ___ of the delegates expressed concerns during the meeting.

questions.def: "Portion" refers to a part of an uncountable noun (land).
questions.question: Only a ___ of the land is suitable for cultivation.

questions.def: "Every" is incorrectly used. Use "Each" instead.
questions.question: Every of the students were given a chance.

questions.def: "Amount" is used with uncountable nouns like "resources" (in general sense).
questions.question: Only a limited ___ of resources are available.

questions.def: "Few" means not many, suitable for countable nouns like "participants".
questions.question: ___ of the participants achieved a perfect score.

questions.def: "Much" is used with uncountable nouns like "rainfall".
questions.question: ___ of the rainfall this year has been below average.

questions.def: "Much" refers to a large amount of an uncountable noun (evidence).
questions.question: ___ of the evidence points to his involvement, though indirectly.

questions.def: "A number of" means "several" and takes a plural verb/noun.
questions.question: ___ students failed the exam, which was surprisingly difficult.

questions.def: "Every" must be followed by a singular noun or "one of".
questions.question: Every of the participants received a certificate.
